problems.title: Translate an integer condition

student_facing.problem_statement: Let x be an integer. Write in set-builder notation and then list the set S of values satisfying −3 < x ≤ 4 and x is even. State whether 0 belongs to S and explain the boundary choices.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: The domain is the integers Z. Even means divisible by 2.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

step_by_step_solution: List the integers in the interval: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Retain exactly the multiples of 2: −2, 0, 2, 4.
Write the set-builder condition with the integer domain.
Zero is even because 0=2·0. The strict lower bound excludes −3 and the non-strict upper bound permits 4.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Set-builder notation specifies domain and predicate.
An integer is even iff it equals 2k for some integer k.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Explains conjunction and endpoint meanings. Obtains exactly −2,0,2,4. Interprets zero as an allowed integer.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: Enumerate multiples of 2 first, then filter by the interval.

corrective_followups: What integer multiplied by 2 gives zero?
Does the definition require a positive multiplier?
Is equality allowed at each endpoint?
Which endpoint satisfies both conditions?

problems.title: Describe a relation precisely

student_facing.problem_statement: Let A={1,2,3} and B={2,4,6,8}. Define R from A to B by y=2x. Write R in set-builder and ordered-pair form, state its domain and range, and translate “8 is in the codomain but not the range” into a statement about possible inputs. Is the assignment a function from A to B?
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: An ordered pair is written (input,output). The declared codomain is B.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: R={(x,y)∈A×B:y=2x}={(1,2),(2,4),(3,6)}. Domain A; range {2,4,6}; no x∈A gives y=8; it is a function.
step_by_step_solution: For x=1,2,3, compute 2x=2,4,6.
Collect the three ordered pairs and state the defining condition in A×B.
The first coordinates give A; second coordinates give {2,4,6}.
The equation 2x=8 needs x=4, which is outside A.
Every element of A has exactly one output in B, so R defines a function; unused codomain values are allowed.
formulas_definitions_theorems: A relation from A to B is a subset of A×B.
A function gives each input exactly one output.
Range consists of attained outputs and can be smaller than the codomain.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Cites exactly one output for each input. Lists the three pairs and domain/range correctly. Explains why 8 has no preimage in A.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A mapping diagram or a two-column input-output table is acceptable.

problems.title: One room for each team or one room for all

student_facing.problem_statement: Three teams a,b,c can use rooms 1 and 2. The allowed pairs are R={(a,1),(b,2),(c,1),(c,2)}. Explain the difference between “each team has an allowed room” and “one room is allowed for every team.” Determine which statement is true, and construct a function assigning each team an allowed room. Explain why neither statement requires distinct rooms for different teams.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Several teams may share a room; no capacity constraint is imposed. “One room” means at least one common room, not exactly one.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: ∀t∈{a,b,c} ∃r∈{1,2}: (t,r)∈R is true; ∃r ∀t:(t,r)∈R is false. One valid function is f(a)=1,f(b)=2,f(c)=1. Neither claim asserts injectivity.
step_by_step_solution: Team a has room 1, b has room 2, and c has rooms 1 and 2; thus each team has a witness.
A common room cannot be 1 because b cannot use it, and cannot be 2 because a cannot use it.
Choose one allowed room for each team, for example 1,2,1 respectively.
The assignment is single-valued even though two inputs share output 1.
Exchanging the order of “for every” and “there exists” changes whether the room may depend on the team. Distinctness would require an extra condition f(t)=f(u) implies t=u.
formulas_definitions_theorems: Quantifier order determines dependence of witnesses.
Function does not mean one-to-one function.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Explains dependence of existential choice on universal variable. Supplies witnesses, rejects both common-room candidates and constructs f. Separates single-valuedness from injectivity.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: Use intersections of allowed-room sets: {1}∩{2}∩{1,2}=∅.

corrective_followups: May the chosen room change when the team changes?
Can either room work for all three teams?
Does uniqueness concern outputs per input or inputs per output?
Where was a distinct-room restriction stated?

student_facing.problem_statement: Of 60 students, 34 attended a coding workshop A, 29 attended a statistics workshop B, and 12 attended both. Label all four regions of a two-set Venn diagram, or give an equivalent region table. How many attended exactly one workshop, and how many attended neither?

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: A only=22; B only=17; both=12; neither=9; exactly one=39.

Union=22+12+17=51, equivalently 34+29−12.
Neither=60−51=9.
Exactly one=22+17=39; all four regions sum to 60.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Justifies subtracting overlap. Computes 22,17,12,9 and 39. Distinguishes exactly one from union.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: Use inclusion-exclusion first, then compute the exclusive regions.

problems.title: Prove and compare parity arguments

student_facing.problem_statement: Prove that for every integer n, n² is even if and only if n is even. Use a direct proof for one direction and a contrapositive proof with the even/odd cases for the other. Then explain how the second direction can be written as a proof by contradiction, and why checking many examples is insufficient.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Every integer is either even (2k) or odd (2k+1) for some integer k. A biconditional requires both directions.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: If n=2k, n²=2(2k²) is even. If n is odd, n²=2(2k²+2k)+1 is odd; hence n² even implies n even. Assuming n² even and n odd yields a contradiction.
step_by_step_solution: Direct direction: n even gives n=2k. Squaring gives n²=4k²=2(2k²); the parenthesized quantity is an integer.
For the reverse direction, use the contrapositive n odd implies n² odd.
The exhaustive parity cases leave n=2k+1 when n is not even. Squaring gives 4k²+4k+1=2(2k²+2k)+1, an odd integer.
Thus an even square cannot come from an odd integer, so the original reverse implication follows.
As a contradiction proof, assume n² even and n not even. The odd case forces n² odd, contradicting its evenness.
Both directions hold for arbitrary integers, including negative integers and zero. Finite examples cannot establish an infinite universal claim.

instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Explains logical equivalence of a statement and its contrapositive. Derives both square forms with integer witnesses. Describes the incompatible even and odd conclusion under contradiction.
instructor_only.alternative_methods: A full even/odd case proof is valid; still explain the direct, contrapositive and contradiction forms requested.

problems.title: Repeated letters without adjacent vowels

student_facing.problem_statement: How many distinct arrangements of the letters in BANANA have no two A letters adjacent? Give a counting argument that handles the repeated N letters and prove that the construction counts each valid arrangement exactly once.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: There are three identical A letters, two identical N letters and one B. Arrangements are linear strings, not circular.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: 12 distinct arrangements.
step_by_step_solution: Arrange the non-A letters B,N,N in 3!/2!=3 distinct orders.
Each order creates four gaps: before, between consecutive letters, and after.
To avoid adjacent As, put at most one A in a gap; choose 3 of the 4 gaps in C(4,3)=4 ways.
The three A letters are identical, so there is no additional factor 3!.

student_facing.problem_statement: Compare two complete small datasets A={−1,−1,1,1} and B={−2,0,0,2}. For each compute the mean and central moments m2,m3,m4, where mr=(1/n)Σ(x−mean)^r. Then compute g1=m3/(m2^(3/2)), kurtosis β2=m4/m2² and excess kurtosis β2−3. Evaluate: “Zero skewness proves normality” and “The dataset with larger variance must have larger standardized kurtosis.”
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Use unadjusted empirical moments with denominator n, not bias-adjusted software estimators. These are descriptive datasets, not normality tests.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: A: mean=0,m2=1,m3=0,m4=1,g1=0,β2=1,excess=−2. B: mean=0,m2=2,m3=0,m4=8,g1=0,β2=2,excess=−1. Both claims are false in general; zero skewness alone does not prove normality, and scaling changes variance but not standardized kurtosis.
step_by_step_solution: Both datasets have mean zero and symmetric values, so their cubic moments cancel to zero.
For A, squared and fourth powers all equal 1, hence m2=m4=1 and β2=1.

student_facing.problem_statement: Four independent service tickets are categorized routine, urgent or specialist with probabilities 0.5,0.3,0.2 respectively. Find the probability of exactly 2 routine, 1 urgent and 1 specialist ticket. Explain why multiplying three independent binomial probabilities for the category counts would be invalid. Independently of the categories, a batch completion time T is normal with mean 30 and standard deviation 5 minutes. Find P(T≤35), P(T=35), and the probability that both the specified category mix occurs and T≤35. Explain the independence assumption needed for the last result.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Ticket categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive for each ticket. Tickets are independent with fixed probabilities. T is independent of the entire category-count vector. Use Φ(1)=0.8413447461 or a standard normal calculator.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Mix probability=4!/(2!1!1!)·0.5²·0.3·0.2=0.18. P(T≤35)=Φ(1)≈0.8413447461; P(T=35)=0; joint probability≈0.1514420543. Counts sum to 4 and are dependent.
step_by_step_solution: Any fixed ordering with the desired mix has probability 0.5²·0.3·0.2=0.015.

Counts are constrained to sum to 4: knowing two determines the third. Although each marginal count is binomial, the three are not independent.
Standardize T: z=(35−30)/5=1, so the cumulative probability is Φ(1).
A continuous normal variable assigns zero probability to an exact point, so P(T=35)=0; a measured rounded value would be a different event.
Independence of time from categories permits 0.18·Φ(1)=0.1514420543 for the joint event. Without it, the time probability conditional on the mix would be required.
formulas_definitions_theorems: A point has probability zero under a continuous density.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Distinguishes independent trials from dependent counts. Computes 0.18,Φ(1),zero and their joint event. Explains exact versus rounded time.

student_facing.problem_statement: Three tools have affordability/support benefit ratings A=(9,5), B=(6,9), C=(8,7). A mandatory accessibility requirement is met by A and B but not C. Use affordability weight w and support weight 1−w, where 0≤w≤1. Derive the preferred eligible tool as a function of w. At w=0.60 compare the correct decision with the ranking obtained if the mandatory requirement were wrongly treated as optional. Is one eligible tool robustly preferred for every w in [0.50,0.70]? Explain how stakeholder interviews should inform the model.
student_facing.given_information_and_assumptions: Weights reflect priorities, not probabilities. Benefit ratings have a common 0–10 scale. Failure of the mandatory requirement makes a tool infeasible regardless of score.
student_facing.response_instruction: Show your reasoning, justify your method, and check your result. Equivalent valid methods are welcome.

instructor_only.expected_final_answer: Eligible A score=5+4w; B=9−3w. B preferred for w<4/7, tie at 4/7, A for w>4/7. At 0.60 choose A (7.4 vs B 7.2); C would score 7.6 but is ineligible. Neither A nor B wins throughout [0.50,0.70].
step_by_step_solution: Apply the mandatory constraint first: remove C from feasible alternatives.
Express scores A=9w+5(1−w)=5+4w and B=6w+9(1−w)=9−3w.
A−B=7w−4, so the switch occurs at w=4/7.
At w=0.60, scores A=7.4,B=7.2,C=7.6. The largest raw score belongs to an infeasible tool and cannot determine the recommendation.
The uncertainty interval spans 4/7: B wins at 0.50 and A at 0.70, so neither wins across the interval.

Interviews can clarify requirements, rating evidence and acceptable trade-offs. They should not convert a mandatory accessibility condition into a compensable preference without authorization; observed preferences alone do not establish a prescriptive requirement.

Robust ranking means the same choice across the specified uncertainty range.
instructor_only.expected_reasoning: Explains noncompensable requirements. Derives threshold 4/7 and scores at 0.60. Explains absence of a robust winner across the range.

A forecast costs 8 and returns positive (+) or negative (−), with P(+|H)=0.8 and P(+|L)=0.2.
